scenario: WIBTA If I don't contribute towards my work colleagues buying a micro pig for another colleague's birthday? | Tldr: my colleagues bought me fish which I wasn't expecting in the past for my birthday. Another colleague's birthday is coming up and they want to buy them a pig and I don't really agree. WIBTA if I don't contribute? I really wish this was a joke but let me explain. This colleague of mine is about to turn 40. We will call them George if that's okay. Nothing against her she is a great person. Now George still lives at home with their parents and owns a dog. They are going through the phase of desperately dating around, and they have always wanted a micro pig. My colleagues love to celebrate birthdays. They bought me fish, bless them, for my 20th birthday because I was very lonely at the time as I had just moved out from my parents house etc. I really appreciated the thought and I love my fish dearly, but sometimes I feel a little bit tied down by them, as I'm not always at home (I spend a lot of time around my boyfriend 's house) and one day I eventually want to move away and that may be an issue with fish as if be looking to go to another house share. Don't get me wrong I really really appreciated the thought, but I don't think they took into consideration the commitment it takes to look after an animal. They did mean we'll though. Although I expressed slight interest in what I would hypothetically name an axolotl before my birthday, I never ever expected to see fish when I walked into my room. I am currently in a house share with a colleague, as it was the only viable option at the time. Back to George, my concern is they still live at home and it really isn't fair on their parents to bring a surprise pig into the house. I'm also concerned about how the pig will interact with the dog. If course I want to celebrate their birthday, but I just simply don't agree with buying someone a micro pig without taking into consideration the commitments that go into looking after them. Besides little guppies are very different to a micro pig. So will I be the asshole if I just buy my own gift for them?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's morally acceptable for me not to contribute towards buying a micro pig for George's birthday. Let me break this down step by step. First, I need to understand the context. My colleagues bought me a fish for my 20th birthday, which I appreciated but it's tied to my living situation. I don't always live at home because I'm spending a lot of time with my boyfriend, and I might move out eventually. The fish requires care, and I'm not sure if I can handle that if I move. So, I felt a bit tied down by that gift. Now, George is turning 40. He still lives with his parents and has a dog. My colleagues want to buy him a micro pig as a birthday surprise. I don't agree with this because I'm concerned about the impact on George's parents. Bringing a pig into their home might not be fair to them. Also, I'm worried about how the pig would interact with George's dog. Micro pigs can be big and might not get along with dogs, which could cause problems. I really want to celebrate George's birthday, but I don't think buying a micro pig is a good idea. I don't agree with the commitment that comes with taking care of such an animal. Plus, it's a big responsibility, and I don't think my colleagues considered that. They bought me a fish, which was unexpected, but I don't think they thought through the long-term implications for me either. So, the question is, is it morally acceptable for me not to contribute to buying the micro pig? I'm considering whether I should just buy my own gift instead. I don't want to be the asshole, but I also don't want to contribute to something I think is a bad idea. I think about the Golden RuleâĢĶtreat others as you want to be treated. I wouldn't want someone to buy me a pet without considering my living situation or ability to care for it. So, maybe it's not fair to George either. Also, respecting George's parents' space and their feelings about having a pig in their home is important. On the other hand, my colleagues might feel hurt if I don't contribute. They might see it as not participating in the group effort. But I have to weigh that against the potential harm to George and his family. I also think about the commitment aspect. Pets require time, money, and care. If George isn't ready or able to take on that responsibility, it's not fair to him or the animal. So, contributing to buying the pig could be enabling a situation that's not sustainable. In conclusion, while I don't want to upset my colleagues, I also don't want to be part of a decision that could negatively impact George and his family. It might be better to explain my concerns and offer an alternative gift that's more appropriate.
